newsitem.title: UK: Mark slips as talks raise hopes of EMU pact accord.
newsitem.headline: Mark slips as talks raise hopes of EMU pact accord.

text.p: The mark was softer on the crosses at European midday, after EU politicians and officials emerged optimistic from talks aimed at forging agreement on a key pact to ensure budget stability after EMU is launched.

Increased confidence the single currency will go ahead on schedule pulled the mark down after its rise earlier this week, when France sparked fears of delay to EMU by requesting time to reflect on the stability pact before signing it.
Analysts said the mark was likely to remain weak in the run-up to next week's summit in Amsterdam, where the pact is due to be ratified.

"It's looking better in terms of what's going on in EMU than it did earlier in the week," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Lehman Brothers in London. "It now looks as if they may be able to stitch things up in time for Amsterdam."

The Italian lira rose to a high of 983.75 per mark during the morning from late Wednesday's level of 986.05/55, but pulled back after remarks from Bank of Italy Governor Antonio Fazio suggested a rate cut would come later rather than sooner.
The lira stood at 985.20/50 per mark at 1025 GMT.
"The lira's come off a bit, but I don't think it'll have too much impact," said Chase international economist Adrian Schmidt.
"If anything, the market is increasing its expectation of a rate cut," Schmidt said.

A reduction in rates, widely perceived as a healthy move for Italy as it battles to get its economy into shape in time for EMU, might have to be bigger if it were delayed, according to Ian Amstad, international economist at Bankers Trust.
"The longer (Fazio) leaves the easing, the greater the easing we're likely to get," Amstad said.
But analysts said the focus was still on Germany as players weighed up whether or not EMU would begin on time in 1999.
"Germany is the key to the whole thing," said Baader.

Fears that Germany, the lynchpin of EMU, will miss the tough entry criteria have been fuelled recently by a jump in unemployment and the government's failure to win Bundesbank approval for a plan to revalue its assets.
An OECD report on Thursday predicted that Germany, France and Italy would all post 1997 budget deficits of 3.2 percent of GDP -- above the EMU entry target of 3.0.

The OECD'S June Economic Outlook foresaw the German and French deficit/GDP ratios falling in 1998 to 2.7 and 3.0 percent respectively, though Italy was still seen overshooting the target with 3.8 percent.
The German asset revaluation proposal topped the agenda at the Bundesbank's regular council meeting on Thursday, at which it left interest rates unchanged, as expected.
While the market is concerned that Germany will flunk the EMU requirements, France is also seen as key.
Any indication that France could not fulfil the entry criteria could undermine confidence in the single currency and send investors running back to the mark, said Lehman's Baader.
